hero_badge: Near-Zero RPO and RTO for Databases
hero_description: Lose a data center without losing committed data or waiting for a war room. KubeDB moves the primary across data centers in about a lease period, supports zero data loss with synchronous replication, and covers PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, MongoDB, OpenSearch, and active-active distributed SQL.
when_to_use_description: RPO is how much committed data you can lose. RTO is how long the database is unavailable. KubeDB lets you pick the point on that curve that fits each database, and then prove it.

when_to_use.title: Near-Zero Data Loss
when_to_use.description: About 5 seconds of RPO with asynchronous replication, and zero with synchronous mode at the cost of one WAN round trip per commit.

when_to_use.title: Failover Without a Human Decision
when_to_use.description: With automatic failover, a lease expiry (45 seconds by default) plus promotion is all it takes. No pager, no runbook.

when_to_use.title: One Operator for Every Engine
when_to_use.description: The same operating model covers PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, MongoDB, and OpenSearch, each with its native cross-DC mechanism.

when_to_use.title: Drill and Prove It
when_to_use.description: Run planned switchovers and quarterly DR drills to measure the RPO and RTO you actually get, not the one on paper.

how_it_works_title: Option A: Automatic Data Center Failover
how_it_works_subtitle: A 3-site etcd quorum decides which data center is primary. Each site follows it, fail-closed, so a failover never waits for a person and never creates two writable primaries.

items.text: One small VM in a third site for the tie-breaking etcd vote
Decide: the hub's etcd holds the primary data center lease (45 s by default)
Project: an addon agent writes a fail-closed marker on each site
Enforce: a cut-off site fences itself, and the coordinator promotes only when the marker names its site and is fresh
HA inside each site, WAL streaming across sites over TLS, and no run-time dependency on the hub for running databases

faqs_subtitle: Everything you need to know about disaster recovery with KubeDB

faqs.question: What RPO and RTO can I expect?
faqs.answer: With automatic failover, RTO is the lease expiry (45 seconds by default) plus promotion. With asynchronous PostgreSQL replication, RPO is about 5 seconds, bounded by a lag guard. With synchronous replication, RPO is zero. Planned switchovers are always zero data loss. Your actual numbers depend on your network and workload, so measure them in a drill.

faqs.question: Which option should I choose?
faqs.answer: Choose Option A (automatic) when a data center failover must not wait for a person, you run many databases, and you can host one small VM in a third site for the tie-breaking vote. Choose Option B (manual) when a human must approve every data center move, you have only two sites, you are migrating into KubeDB, or you want the smallest footprint. Choose active-active distributed SQL for new services that need zero loss and zero downtime and can tolerate the application changes.

faqs.question: What does synchronous replication cost?
faqs.answer: Each commit waits for the standby, so write latency grows by one WAN round trip between the data centers. In exchange, a lost data center loses no committed data. Many teams enable it only for the databases that need it.

faqs.question: When should I use active-active?
faqs.answer: When you need RPO zero and near-zero RTO and can keep data centers within metro latency (around 5 ms). Distributed SQL such as YugabyteDB replicates with Raft, and each data center holds a full copy. It requires application changes, so it is best suited to new services.

faqs.question: Is there always only one writable primary?
faqs.answer: For PostgreSQL, yes. Both options are Active/Standby, because PostgreSQL allows one writable primary. They differ only in how a data center failover is triggered. Active-active distributed SQL is the exception, by design.

faqs.question: Does this cover databases other than PostgreSQL?
faqs.answer: Yes. Redis uses DR replicas with a cluster takeover, Kafka uses MirrorMaker 2 on a ConnectCluster, MongoDB uses non-voting DR members, and OpenSearch uses cross-cluster replication. Cross-DC replication for these engines is asynchronous, so RPO equals replication lag.

faqs.question: How does failover avoid a split brain?
faqs.answer: Option A uses an etcd majority plus a fail-closed marker on each site. A site that loses contact fences itself, and a coordinator promotes only when the marker names its site and is fresh. In Option B, the operator fences the old primary before promoting the new one.

faqs.question: What if the hub is unavailable?
faqs.answer: Running databases do not depend on the hub at run time. Each site keeps serving under its last fail-closed marker, and the hub's etcd quorum is only needed to move the primary.

faqs.question: How many VMs does the Option A hub need?
faqs.answer: Three VMs for development, five for production, and seven for production with availability zones. Every VM needs a routable IP to every other VM, and the tie-breaker site never joins the Kubernetes cluster or runs workloads.

faqs.question: What happens when the old primary comes back?
faqs.answer: It returns as a standby. Option A re-syncs it automatically with pg_rewind or a re-seed. In Option B, you recreate it as a Remote Replica, and with a Halt deletion policy the volumes survive so pg_rewind can repair it in place. Failback repeats the process with the roles swapped.

faqs.question: Does BCDR include backup and point-in-time recovery?
faqs.answer: Yes. KubeDB provides encrypted, incremental backups with point-in-time recovery, so you can recover from failures that replication would copy to the standby, such as an accidental delete.

faqs.question: How do I know my targets are met?
faqs.answer: Run planned switchovers and scheduled DR drills, for example quarterly, and record the RPO and RTO each drill measures. The kubectl dba dc-dr command shows status and progress during every step.

faqs.question: Is this running in production?
faqs.answer: Yes. KubeDB runs a highly available primary cluster with a live DR replica at a geographically separate site for a regulated mobile financial services platform. Read the TeleCash case study for details.
